questions.q: What does the differencing order d represent in ARIMA(p,d,q)?
options: The number of times the series is differenced before fitting the ARMA part
The number of moving average lags
questions.explain: d counts how many times the series is differenced (x_t minus x_(t-1), repeated) to remove trends or unit roots, after which an ARMA(p,q) model is fit to the differenced series.

questions.q: Why does statsmodels implement ARMA and ARIMA with the same ARIMA class?
options: Because ARMA and ARIMA require completely different estimation algorithms that happen to share a name
Because ARMA is simply ARIMA with d=0 — no differencing applied
Because statsmodels does not actually support ARMA models
Because d always equals p in practice
questions.explain: ARIMA(p, d, q) with d=0 performs no differencing, which is mathematically identical to ARMA(p, q). statsmodels uses one class to express both.

questions.q: A series is differenced twice (d=2) but the fitted residuals show a strong negative MA(1) pattern. What does this most likely indicate?
options: The series needed a third difference
The model has too few AR terms
questions.explain: A strong negative MA(1) signature in the residuals is a classic sign of over-differencing — differencing more times than the series actually needs to become stationary.

questions.q: In SARIMA(p,d,q)(P,D,Q)_s with s=12, what does the seasonal AR term P actually operate on?
options: Only the very first 12 observations in the dataset
questions.explain: The seasonal part of SARIMA operates at lag multiples of the seasonal period s. With s=12, the seasonal AR/MA terms reference lags 12, 24, 36, and so on, capturing year-over-year dynamics in monthly data.

questions.q: Which statsmodels class is used to fit a SARIMA model with seasonal_order=(1,1,1,12)?
questions.explain: statsmodels.tsa.statespace.sarimax.SARIMAX implements seasonal ARIMA, accepting both order=(p,d,q) and seasonal_order=(P,D,Q,s); the 'X' refers to optional exogenous regressors, which can be omitted.
